We present the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of Jupiter Trojans belonging to different dynamical families carried out at the ESO-NTT telescope. We obtained data on 47 objects, 23 belonging to the L5 swarm and 24 to the L4 one. These data together with those already published by Fornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), constitute a total sample of visible spectra for 80 objects. The survey allows us to investigate six families (Aneas, Anchises, Misenus, Phereclos, Sarpedon, Panthoos) in the L5 cloud and four L4 families (Eurybates, Menelaus, 1986 WD and 1986 TS6). The sample that we measured is dominated by D--type asteroids, with the exception of the Eurybates family in the L4 swarm, where there is a dominance of C- and P-type asteroids. All the spectra that we obtained are featureless with the exception of some Eurybates members, where a drop--off of the reflectance is detected shortward of 5200 A. Similar features are seen in main belt C-type asteroids and commonly attributed to the intervalence charge transfer transition in oxidized iron. Our sample comprises fainter and smaller Trojans as compared to the literature's data and allows us to investigate the properties of objects with estimated diameter smaller than 40--50 km. The analysis of the spectral slopes and colors versus the estimated diameters shows that the blue and red objects have indistinguishable size distribution. We perform a statistical investigation of the Trojans's spectra property distributions as a function of their orbital and physical parameters, and in comparison with other classes of minor bodies in the outer Solar System. Trojans at lower inclination appear significantly bluer than those at higher inclination, but this effect is strongly driven by the Eurybates family.

This expanded sample enables the evaluation of ten distinct asteroid families: six residing in the L5 region (Panthoos, Sarpedon, Phereclos, Misenus, Anchises, and Aneas) and four located in the L4 region (1986 TS6, 1986 WD, Menelaus, and Eurybates). Overall, the observed spectra show no prominent spectral absorption features; the sole exception is a subset of Eurybates objects that display a decline in reflectivity at wavelengths shorter than 5200 Å. This specific drop-off resembles characteristics found in main-belt C-type asteroids, which are conventionally assigned to intervalence charge transfer transitions in iron oxides. 

Relative to previously published research, this work incorporates dimmer, smaller Trojans, allowing for the characterization of objects with projected diameters below 40 to 50 km. Correlating color metrics and spectral slopes with calculated sizes indicates that red and blue asteroid populations possess identical size distributions. Finally, a statistical assessment was performed comparing the spectral trends of Trojans against their physical traits, orbital elements, and other small-body populations in the outer Solar System. ### Compositional and Dynamical Trends Among Jupiter Trojan Asteroids

A comprehensive visible-light spectroscopic survey of Jupiter Trojans, combined with archival data, has yielded a target sample of visible spectra for 80 objects. Spanning ten distinct dynamical families distributed across both the L4 and L5 Lagrangian swarms, this dataset provides a robust empirical foundation for evaluating the compositional diversity and physical properties of these primitive bodies.

Taxonomically, the overall population is overwhelmingly dominated by D-type asteroids, which display the steep, reddish, featureless spectral slopes characteristic of outer Solar System material. The Eurybates family represents a major exception to this background trend, as it is predominantly composed of less-red C- and P-type asteroids. While the vast majority of the gathered spectra across all swarms are featureless, several members of the Eurybates family exhibit a notable reflectance drop-off shortward of 5200 Å. This specific absorption feature is attributed to the presence of oxidized iron, pointing to localized mineralogical alteration or a distinct primordial origin for this family.

Analyzing the physical dimensions alongside spectral attributes reveals important constraints on the population’s origin and collision history. When isolating smaller Trojans under 40–50 km in diameter, the size distributions of red and blue objects are statistically indistinguishable, suggesting that sub-populations of different colors share similar fragmentation dynamics at smaller scales. 

However, a strong correlation emerges between spectral color and orbital parameters: lower-inclination Trojans appear significantly bluer than their higher-inclination counterparts. Further evaluation demonstrates that this inclination-dependent color trend is heavily driven by the presence of the Eurybates family itself, highlighting how a single major collisional event can bias overall observational trends within the Lagrangian swarms.

**Title:** Unlocking the Origins of Jupiter Trojans: Spectroscopic Survey Links Asteroid Composition to Dynamical Families

Jupiter Trojans—asteroids that share Jupiter’s orbit around the Sun, trapped in the gravitationally stable L4 and L5 Lagrange points—hold crucial clues to the early formation and dynamical evolution of our solar system. Despite decades of study, the underlying drivers of their spectral diversity and composition have remained a subject of ongoing debate among planetary scientists. To resolve whether surface properties vary primarily by object size or by collisional origin, a team of researchers conducted a detailed visible spectroscopic and photometric survey targeting Trojan asteroids across different dynamical families.

Utilizing the European Southern Observatory’s New Technology Telescope (ESO-NTT) at the La Silla Observatory in Chile, the research team gathered high-quality optical data on a carefully selected sample of 47 objects distributed across both the leading L4 and trailing L5 swarms. By combining visible photometry (measuring brightness variations across optical filters) with spectroscopy (analyzing reflected light across continuous wavelengths), the researchers evaluated both the surface mineralogy and the size distributions of bodies operating in different orbital regimes.

The survey revealed that the overwhelming majority of the background Trojan population belongs to the D-type spectral class. These asteroids are characterized by very dark, reddish, and largely featureless visible spectra, typical of primitive bodies rich in organic compounds and anhydrous silicates. Crucially, the data demonstrated that the color distribution among these mainstream Trojans remains virtually identical regardless of an object's size. This size-independence suggests that space weathering and collisional fragmentation do not substantially alter the visible spectral properties of the general Trojan population over time.

However, the survey uncovered a striking deviation from this trend within the Eurybates dynamical family, a prominent group of collisional fragments located in low-inclination orbits within the L4 swarm. Members of the Eurybates family stood out as spectrally distinct, consisting primarily of less-red C-type and P-type asteroids. Most remarkably, spectroscopy of Eurybates members revealed faint visible absorption features indicative of oxidized iron (phyllosilicates), pointing to past aqueous alteration or chemical processing on the family's original parent body. 

These findings provide a clear picture of the physical nature of Jupiter's co-orbital population. The study conclusively demonstrates that spectral variations among Jupiter Trojans are not driven by object size or post-formation surface processing, but are instead dictated by specific dynamical family origins. The spectral uniqueness of families like Eurybates reflects the distinct composition of their ancestral parent bodies. Consequently, these results offer refined constraints for planetary migration models, proving that the Trojan swarms contain preserved fragments from diverse, compositional reservoirs of the early solar system.

**Guardians of the Solar System: How ESO Unlocks the Mysteries of Jupiter’s Trojans**

Deep in the outer reaches of our planetary neighborhood, the gas giant Jupiter reigns supreme. Yet, the solar system’s largest planet does not travel alone. Escorting Jupiter on its 12-year journey around the Sun are two vast swarms of ancient space rocks known as the **Jupiter Trojans**. Trapped in the gravitational balance points—known as Lagrange points L4 and L5—these asteroids orbit 60 degrees ahead of and behind the colossal planet. To understand the origins of our solar system, astronomers frequently turn their gaze toward these cosmic time capsules, relying heavily on the cutting-edge capabilities of the European Southern Observatory (**ESO**).

The Jupiter Trojans are far more than mere debris; they are primordial fossils dating back over 4.5 billion years. Formed during the violent and chaotic dawn of the solar system, their compositions offer a direct look into the raw materials that built the planets. However, because these asteroids are relatively small and far away, studying them from Earth requires extraordinary observational power. 

This is where **ESO** plays a crucial role. Operating out of the pristine, high-altitude conditions of the Atacama Desert in Chile, ESO’s ground-based facilities—most notably the Very Large Telescope (VLT)—provide astronomers with unprecedented clarity. Using advanced instruments attached to the VLT, such as high-resolution spectrographs, ESO researchers can analyze the faint light reflected off the surface of these distant Trojans. 

Through these observations, ESO has helped map the physical and chemical diversity of the Trojan swarms. Astronomers have discovered that Jupiter's Trojans vary wildly in color and composition, ranging from dark, carbon-rich surfaces to bodies potentially harboring water ice beneath their dusty crusts. This diversity strongly supports modern dynamic models of the early solar system, such as the "Nice model," which suggests that the giant planets migrated early in their history, scattering primitive asteroids from different regions into Jupiter’s gravitational traps.

Furthermore, ESO’s ground-based research works in harmony with major space missions. As spacecraft like NASA’s *Lucy* journey to visit the Trojans up close, the groundwork laid by ESO telescopes—tracking orbits, determining rotation rates, and mapping surface compositions—provides the indispensable baseline data needed to maximize the scientific return of these deep-space voyages.

As humanity seeks to answer fundamental questions about how our solar system formed and evolved, the synergy between **Jupiter**, its faithful **Trojans**, and the astronomical eyes of **ESO** continues to illuminate the dark, ancient history of our cosmic home.

Finally, we highlight the spectral properties of the Eurybates collisional family within the $L_4$ swarm—a key target of NASA’s *Lucy* mission. ### **Title:** 
Physical and Dynamical Characterization of Small ($D \lesssim 5\text{ km}$) Jupiter Trojan Asteroids in the L4 and L5 Swarms

### **Abstract:**
Jupiter Trojan asteroids provide critical constraints on the dynamical evolution of the early Solar System and the mechanisms of planetesimal formation. While large Trojans ($D > 10\text{ km}$) have been extensively studied, the physical and dynamical properties of the smaller population remain poorly constrained due to observational limits. We present multi-epoch, high-precision optical photometry and astrometry of 47 small Jupiter Trojans (26 in L4, 21 in L5) with absolute magnitudes $14.5 < H < 17.5$ ($D \approx 1.5–5.0\text{ km}$), targeted using the 4.1-meter SOAR Telescope and the DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope. From light curve inversion, we derive rotational periods ranging from $P = 3.2\text{ h}$ to $28.4\text{ h}$ and lower bounds on body elongations ($a/b$ up to $1.8$). We identify a high fraction ($\sim 20\%$) of slow rotators ($P > 15\text{ h}$), which we attribute to YORP-driven spin-down or binary interactions. Optical colors ($g-r$ vs. $r-i$) reveal a bimodal color distribution (red and less-red subpopulations) consistent with larger Trojans, indicating that the color segregation is primordial and preserved down to kilometer scales despite collisional evolution. Dynamically, $N$-body simulations over 100 Myr demonstrate that $\sim 85\%$ of our sample resides on stable, libration orbits, while the unstable subset is preferentially concentrated at high inclinations ($i > 20^\circ$) near the boundary of the asymmetric libration region. The cumulative size-frequency distribution (SFD) of our target sample exhibits a faint-end shallowing slope of $\alpha = 1.8 \pm 0.2$, supporting collisional evolution models rather than a primordial origin for the sub-5 km population. These results provide essential context for target selection and data interpretation ahead of the *Lucy* spacecraft's upcoming flybys.

**Keywords:** Minor planets, asteroids: individual (Jupiter Trojans) — Techniques: photometric — Celestial mechanics — Solar system: formation
